articles.title: A wildlife charity bought 335 hectares in Dorset; two years later, it is one of England’s newest National Nature Reserves
articles.summary: In March 2024, Dorset Wildlife Trust and Natural England acquired 335 hectares of chalk downland and farmland at Lyscombe, around 10 miles north-east of
articles.body: In March 2024, Dorset Wildlife Trust and Natural England acquired 335 hectares of chalk downland and farmland at Lyscombe, around 10 miles north-east of Dorchester. The former organically managed farm was acquired for nature conservation and environmental restoration, with funding from Natural England’s National Nature Reserves programme and its planned nutrient mitigation credit scheme, alongside donations from Dorset Wildlife Trust members and supporters. In 2026, Lyscombe became the 16th site in the King’s Series of National Nature Reserves. Natural England formally declared the reserve on 17 August, while its new status was publicly announced and celebrated on 15 September. The formal declaration covers 333.57 hectares, while Dorset Wildlife Trust describes the original acquisition as 335 hectares. The landscape includes chalk grassland, wildflower meadows, scrub, ancient woodland and historic features, with restoration work focused on restoring habitats and creating better-connected spaces for wildlife.From farmland to National Nature ReserveThe new status was celebrated at Lyscombe on 15 September, when Jaqueline Swift, Deputy Lord-Lieutenant of Dorset, represented His Majesty the King at an event attended by Tony Juniper, Chair of Natural England, and Lisbet Sherlock, Chair of Dorset Wildlife Trust. Swift and Juniper unveiled the National Nature Reserve plaque, while Juniper presented Sherlock and Dorset Wildlife Trust chief executive Brian Bleese with the certificate recognising Lyscombe’s new status. The legal declaration had been made on 17 August 2026 under the Wildlife and Countryside Act 1981. The reserve includes 50 hectares of nationally important chalk downland designated as a Site of Special Scientific Interest, as well as a Site of Nature Conservation Interest and several protected heritage features. Among them is Lyscombe Chapel, a Grade II* listed building that dates from the 12th century but was partly rebuilt in the 15th and 16th centuries. Historic England records substantial medieval fabric, including a 12th-century chancel. The nearby ruins of the Priest’s House date from the 16th century.Restoring the chalk grassland and Little PiddleThe conservation work began before the National Nature Reserve designation. Dorset Wildlife Trust says it has removed up to 23 kilometres of outdated fencing and introduced English Longhorn cattle onto the SSSI chalk grassland. The grazing is intended to maintain the open character of the chalk grassland, prevent scrub encroachment and support biodiversity. The Trust is also pursuing restoration of the Little Piddle, which rises at Lyscombe and is a tributary of the River Piddle. Its plans include returning the stream towards a more natural course, removing concrete culverts and outdated agricultural infrastructure, and creating wetland habitat and fen meadows in the valley bottom. Dorset Wildlife Trust says that changing land management and creating new wetland habitat at Lyscombe will help reduce harmful nutrient inputs into the Poole Harbour catchment, while Natural England says the project has contributed to reducing historic pollution in the local River Piddle. The acquisition was also partly funded through Natural England’s nutrient mitigation scheme, linking the land purchase to wider efforts to reduce nutrient pollution in the Poole Harbour catchment.Monitoring a landscape in transitionDorset Wildlife Trust is carrying out ecological, soil and hydrological surveys to establish baselines and guide future management, with monitoring covering invertebrates, small mammals, bats, breeding birds and flora. In 2025, the Trust worked with the Environmental Sensing department at the University of Southampton to enable a student to create a virtual tour of Lyscombe using ArcGIS StoryMaps. The project incorporated drone data collected at the site and included a 3D model of the landscape. The Trust also reports that barn owls have returned since the acquisition, which it links to a resurgence of small mammals in the fields and hedgerows. That is an observation reported by the Trust rather than an independent assessment of the cause. Alongside the ecological work, Dorset Wildlife Trust is working with Historic England on heritage features including the chapel and the ruined Priest’s House, while also planning restoration of existing barns. The project therefore combines habitat restoration and wildlife monitoring with the protection of a landscape containing significant archaeological and historic features.A long-term project beyond the reserveLyscombe’s National Nature Reserve designation gives national recognition to a project that began with the 2024 acquisition, but the restoration itself is intended to continue for years. Natural England describes the reserve as 334 hectares and says it has potential to contribute to nature recovery across the wider 5,700-hectare Dorset Downs landscape. Dorset Wildlife Trust’s plans combine conservation management of the existing SSSI with natural regeneration and a rewilding approach across wider parts of the site. The Trust says the land is likely to develop into a mosaic of grassland, scrub and wood pasture, supported by appropriate grazing and natural regeneration. Lyscombe already supports at least six orchid species, including pyramidal and bee orchids, as well as chalkhill blue butterflies and other wildlife. The reserve’s new status does not mark the completion of that work. Instead, it formally recognises the national importance of the landscape while Dorset Wildlife Trust continues its longer-term programme of habitat restoration, ecological monitoring, conservation grazing and work to reconnect Lyscombe with the wider Dorset Downs.You use AI every day. articles.title: In 1996, a German psychotherapist gave away her possessions and began living without money; what began as a one-year experiment lasted 17 years
articles.summary: Discover the inspiring story of Heidemarie Schwermer, a psychotherapist who lived without money for 17 years, exploring the possibilities of a moneyless life and the implications of trust and community.
articles.body: Most of us would find it hard to get through a weekend without spending. Bus fares, groceries, phone credit and rent are so ingrained into daily life that to imagine living without them seems like a stunt. But in the 1990s a psychotherapist in the German city of Dortmund decided to test the idea properly. In 1996, Heidemarie Schwermer gave away most of her belongings, gave up her flat and stopped using money, initially for a single year. The year went by, and she carried on. Her story is told in Living Without Money, a 2010 documentary by Norwegian filmmaker Line Halvorsen. By then, Schwermer was 68 and 14 years into the experiment, though the film says she lived almost without money, not entirely without it.How a swap shop gave birth to the experimentBorn in Memel, East Prussia, in 1942, Schwermer fled west with her family at the age of two. She started out as a primary school teacher in Kiel in 1965. In 1982 she left the classroom, studied psychology and sociology, trained as a Gestalt psychotherapist and set up a practice in Dortmund. She observed the number of people living in poverty on the streets. In 1994 she established a swap centre called Gib und Nimm, or Give and Take, where people could swap goods and skills without using cash. It was one of the first exchange circles of this kind in Germany.Money, she has said, made her uneasy and could come between people. As the swap centre grew, she needed less cash herself, and two years after opening it she decided to find out what life would be like with none.Life without a purseAfter 1996 she had no home of her own. She house-sat for friends who were away, later stayed with members of the swap circle and took on jobs such as gardening, babysitting, cleaning and cooking. At one point she was offered a bed, shower and computer access at a student residence in return for cooking for the young people who lived there. She kept only a few clothes and personal items, and she travelled, speaking about how she lived. She summed up her outlook as having nothing yet being a great deal, according to the organisation Moneyless.org. After four years she felt richer than she had ever been. Not everyone bought it. The film itself says that some people who met her called her a parasite and got furious, while others called her a visionary. She relied entirely on host generosity for her way of life, which is what made it inspiring to some and uncomfortable to others.What she left behindShe wrote about the experience in Das Sterntalerexperiment (2001), a book named after the Grimm fairy tale about a girl who gives away everything she owns. Her German publisher characterises the book as an example of hope rather than a rule for all. According to Books on Demand, which publishes an English edition of her story, she received the Tiziano Terzani Peace Prize in 2008 for the Italian translation.Accounts of how long the experiment ran differ. A 2015 interview with Der Freitag put it at almost 19 years, while the publisher of her book says she lived without money from 1996 until her death in 2016. Either way, it was far longer than the one year she had planned.Her swap-shop idea, though, was easy to copy, she told the German weekly Der Freitag in 2015, citing a friend who had launched a Give and Take shop in Mainz. Perhaps that’s the more valuable legacy. Schwermer showed how much of ordinary life may be arranged by trading and trust, and she made the case by living it far longer than anyone expected.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: In 1964, a Virginia widow fought to save her Frank Lloyd Wright home from Interstate 66; it was dismantled piece by piece, moved 13 miles and rebuilt at Woodlawn, where it still stands
articles.summary: Sixty years ago, a house was reconstructed at Woodlawn, a National Trust-owned property outside of Washington, DC, after a historic and hard-fought battle
articles.body: Sixty years ago, a house was reconstructed at Woodlawn, a National Trust-owned property outside of Washington, DC, after a historic and hard-fought battle to save it from destruction. Originally built in Falls Church, Virginia for Loren and Charlotte Pope, the 1,200-square-foot Frank Lloyd Wright home was under threat due to the construction of the new Interstate 66, but was saved by a historic hard-fought battle led by Marjorie Leighey, a 57-year-old widow, according to the National Trust for Historic Preservation. Today, thousands of guests visit the unique house, the only property designed by America's greatest architect that is open to the public in the National Capital region.A dream houseIt was in 1939 that Loren Pope wrote to the architect Frank Lloyd Wright, begging him for a home for himself and his wife Charlotte. In response, Wright designed a house in his Usonian style- relatively small, built from everyday materials like wood and concrete and designed in harmony with natural surroundings.At the end of 1946, after living in the house for five years, the Popes put a for-sale ad in the papers and two weeks later, the house came to be owned by Robert and Marjorie Leighey. While Robert was the one who first fell in love with the house, his wife, Marjorie, remained sceptical.She was eventually won over by the way the home married the interior and exterior and as an avid gardener, she loved the way the house allowed her to see the surrounding landscape through a new lens. “From the time I was five, I can remember wanting a house that was right with the earth,” she later said. They built a shed outside for items that could not fit in the houseIn 1961, the couple learnt that the new Interstate Highway 66 would pass directly through the property they had lived in for the past 15 years. This meant the government planned to seize their land and demolish their house. But all the concerns were put on the back burner as Robert battled an illness that eventually led to his death on July 29, 1963.Two months after Robert died, Marjorie was officially notified by Virginia's Department of Highways that the interstate was slated to be paved through her living room. Springing into action, she hired a lawyer to delay the government and recognising the abode's cultural importance, asked help from Terry and Hamilton Morton, preservationists who worked for the National Trust for Historic Preservation. At the time, the preservation community tended to focus on saving much older properties, but Marjorie insisted that the 22-year-old house deserved the same protections as properties built 150 years earlier.“It does seem like at least part of her thought in wanting to save the house was also saving memories she has of her husband,” observed Elizabeth Reese, senior manager of public programs at Woodlawn and the Pope-Leighey House. “That demonstrates that for a lot of people, doing larger acts of public service comes from a very personal place.”Saving a homeAlong with Marjorie, preservationists, National Park Service employees, politicians and neighbours all came together to find a way to ensure that the Pope-Leighey House lived on. Recognising the value in gathering public support, Marjorie encouraged the press coverage, giving interviews that pressed for others to join her cause. “I’m not doing this for myself, but for architects, students, and people building their own homes,” she told the Virginia Sun in 1964. Loren Pope now begged the community to stop the destruction of an architectural treasure. In a letter to the editor of the Washington Post, he wrote that only a society with a “barbarian set of values…could even entertain a proposal to let a road threaten [a Wright house].”One of the people inspired by Marjorie’s determination was Secretary of the Interior Stewart Udall. It was he and Marjorie, along with preservationists from the National Park Service and the National Trust for Historic Preservation, who finally devised a plan for saving the Pope-Leighy House.The group quickly realised that while the I-66 plans could not change, the house itself could be moved. After being offered various options, Marjorie chose Woodlawn as its new location, in part because the landscape reminded her of Falls Church. Brick by brick, the house was carefully demolished, transported, and rebuilt on the National Trust property, where Marjorie lived in it until her death. The near-loss of the Pope-Leighey House was one of many efforts that inspired Udall and preservationists across the country to pursue a national law to preserve historic buildings. Thanks in part to his and Marjorie’s efforts, President Johnson signed the National Historic Preservation Act in 1966.A lasting legacyAfter fighting for so long to ensure the survival of her home, Marjorie moved to Kyoto, Japan, to become an Episcopal missionary in September 1964, and did not witness the dismantling, move, and reconstruction of her house 13 miles away from Falls Church to Alexandria.Just seven years later, the house was listed on the National Register. Marjorie moved back to the country and to her home in 1969. She continued to live in it until her death, and welcomed the many visitors who came to see not only the house, but the woman who saved it.Thanks to Marjorie Leighey's efforts and the tools instituted by the National Historic Preservation Act, dozens of sites of cultural and historical significance have been saved, both by individuals and government entities. “She was an accidental preservationist,” Reese said. “Hopefully, when people visit this exhibit, [they ask themselves], ‘what kinds of personal things can I do that might make a larger impact?’ “You use AI every day. articles.title: St. Anthony Village buried a 500,000-gallon tank beside a Minnesota road; it now catches runoff and reuses the water to irrigate City Park and City Hall
articles.summary: St. Anthony Village has constructed a groundbreaking 500,000-gallon tank to capture and reuse stormwater runoff for irrigation at City Hall and Central Park, significantly reducing pollution and groundwater usage.
articles.body: Rain washes pollutants from roads into the stormwater system. Along the way, runoff can pick up debris, oil, litter and leaves before entering the stormwater system. It was intercepted by St. Anthony Village, a small town in the Twin Cities region of Minnesota. St. Anthony Village installed a 500,000-gallon underground storage tank that collects runoff from nearby streets, buildings and parking lots. It collects runoff from nearby streets and parking lots and stores it for later reuse.According to the City of St. Anthony Village, the facility was the first of its kind when installed. The city reports a 91% reduction in runoff volume during the growing season, a 77.5% reduction in phosphorus load from the site and savings of about 4.6 million gallons of potable water or groundwater for irrigation each year.Why runoff is a problemThe city says stormwater runoff is a major source of pollution to surface waters, while runoff from rooftops, pavement and lawns can carry garbage, oil and debris into storm drains and nearby water bodies. Silver Lake is on Minnesota’s Impaired Waters List, and stormwater systems in St. Anthony and surrounding communities can carry runoff directly into local lakes, rivers and streams. Phosphorus is of particular concern since it feeds the algae in lakes, and the city is responsible for two watersheds that expect to see continuous improvement.What the tank doesThe system, which catches, cleans and reuses runoff from a 15-acre area around City Hall, was funded by the Mississippi Watershed Management Organisation. Water is stored in a 500,000-gallon underground reservoir before being reused on about 20 acres of municipal land. The city calls that park Central Park, but some state documents call it City Park.The tank has another function: it also receives backwash from the adjacent water treatment plant and filters that water for reuse. Solid pollutants settle to the bottom of the tank, while the stored water is filtered and then pumped to the adjacent ball fields and City Hall campus for irrigation. A Metropolitan Council handbook gives the city's water tower a capacity of 250,000 gallons, half the capacity of the underground reservoir.Maintenance and LessonsIf pollution settles out, that means the tank collects it. When the city drained the tank for maintenance in November 2015, it took days to pump the water down and left thigh-thick sludge on the floor, the mayor subsequently wrote. It also shows that the system requires regular cleaning.Minnesota's Stormwater Manual uses St. Anthony Village as a large-scale example of stormwater reuse and notes that stored water from cisterns can be used for non-potable purposes such as irrigation. The same guidance cites Tucson, Arizona, as a separate example, where commercial developments are required to meet at least half of their irrigation needs with harvested rainwater. The project shows how captured stormwater can be reused for municipal irrigation while reducing demand for other water supplies. It does need frequent cleaning and room to grow, but the city’s own results suggest it has been worth the investment.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: In 2020, researchers compressed sand with only about 10% polyethylene; their structural material achieved flexural strength comparable to typical steel-reinforced concrete in tests
articles.summary: Researchers have demonstrated that a composite material made of sand and only 10% polyethylene achieves flexural strength surpassing that of conventional steel-reinforced concrete, paving the way for sustainable building solutions using waste plastics.
articles.body: Researchers in 2020 developed a structural material through the combination of sand with only about 10 wt% polyethylene and compacting the mixture under pressure. The study published as “Sand-Filler Structural Material with Low Content of Polyethylene Binder,” showed by using about 10 wt% polyethylene and 70–100 MPa of compaction pressure, the formulation produced flexural strength greater than typical steel-reinforced concrete.In lieu of using Portland cement, polyethylene, a common plastic, was used to bind sand particles together. The idea behind this approach was to reduce the amount of polymer normally required in constructing plastic based materials and to determine if it was possible to create a different route for recycling waste plastics. The polyethylene particles used were around 40-50 micrometers in size and sand which met the required ASTM C33/33M. The binder content was varied from 4 wt% to 30 wt%, while compaction pressure ranged from 70 MPa to 350 MPa.How the sand-polyethylene material was made The sand and polyethylene (PE) particles were manually mixed before being placed in a steel mold heated at about 200°C, it was then subjected to compaction pressures ranging from 70 to 350 MPa. To distribute the binder, researchers weren’t reliant on extensive mechanical mixing which made the process different from when using conventional polymer cement. Under pressure, the sand grains started to shift, rotate, deform slightly, and drove the melted polyethylene towards the contact points between neighboring grains.Following this arrangement allowed a small amount to contribute largely to the strength of the material. Researchers observed that, at 4 wt% polyethylene, the material would reach about 8 MPa, giving it nearly twice the strength of typical concrete. Going up to 7 wt% increased the flexural strength to around 14 MPa, comparable to any steel-reinforced concrete and at 10 wt%, it rose sharply to 23 MPa.Beyond the 10 wt% threshold, further additions of polyethylene yielded smaller gains in structural reinforcement. Though the material achieved its highest strength of 30 MPa, at 25 wt% PE. Raising the pressure from 70 MPa to 140 MPa increased strength from around 22 MPa to 27 MPa, marking an improvement of nearly 22% but when it went above 140 MPa, then it didn’t produce any additional strengthening. The study identified that the preferred range for production was a 7–10 wt% polyethylene and compaction pressure of 70–100 MPa.The materials’ performance was determined by heating and processingThe final materials properties were significantly influenced by both temperature and processing duration. Before compaction, the samples were heated at 200°C and by increasing the heating duration from 10 to 30 minutes enhanced the material's strength from 14 MPa to 25 MPa, giving a 79% increase. In contrast, longer heating at 50-60 minutes would reduce the strength to around 14 MPa, as observed by researchers this decline was because of oxidation and possibly the polyethylene’s thermal decomposition, which can reduce the effective molecular weight of the polymer.The time between removing the heated mould from the oven and beginning compaction was also important. An interval of less than one minute yielded the highest strength and three to six minutes would level the strength at only 40-60% of the peak value, while an interval of ten minutes would reduce the strength by 80%. The study also found that if the materials were confined when heated, the material’s strength would reduce by 25% which meant that free expansion during heating allowed polyethylene to spread through the sand structure. This approach speaks to the issue of Portland cement production being carbon-intensive, and waste plastics are difficult to recycle. Since building materials are tolerant to minor impurities, the researchers proposed that waste plastic could potentially be used as a binder.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: In 2019, Los Angeles tested a road mix made from old asphalt and recycled plastic bottles, aiming to repave streets without adding new asphalt
articles.summary: In 2019, Los Angeles tested a groundbreaking road recycling method utilizing old asphalt and recycled plastic bottles to pave its streets more sustainably. Learn about this innovative procedure that could revolutionize road construction and reduce emissions.
articles.body: A road rebuilt largely from the material already beneath it sounds straightforward, but conventional resurfacing often involves removing old material, hauling it away and bringing in fresh asphalt. According to Fast Company, in 2019, Los Angeles began testing a different approach: grind up the existing road, add a synthetic binder made partly from recycled plastic bottles and lay the material back down.The pilot was based on a simple idea. Instead of treating the old road as waste and relying on new petroleum-based bitumen to bind recycled pavement, the existing asphalt could be processed in place and held together with a binder derived from recycled polyethene terephthalate, or PET. The proposed system therefore combined two waste materials, old pavement and discarded plastic bottles, in one road-recycling process.Turning old asphalt and bottles into a new roadThis approach, which was developed by TechniSoil Industrial, involved the use of what the company referred to as a continuous recycling train. First, the equipment mills the surface of the old road and crushes the asphalt to the required size. It was then mixed with a liquid synthetic binder, which had been produced using recycled PET and laid down on the road again. This method differs from conventional resurfacing because the top layer of the old road can be recycled without being removed and replaced with new hot-mix asphalt.According to Construction and Building Materials, research on plastic-modified asphalt has found that the behaviour of the finished pavement depends on factors such as the type of plastic, the amount used and the way it is incorporated. PET is among the plastics investigated for improving properties such as stability, although researchers also note that high plastic contents can affect other characteristics of an asphalt mixture. The Los Angeles experiment was therefore not simply a matter of mixing shredded bottles into ordinary asphalt. The plastic was processed into a synthetic binder that served a different function in the road material.A pilot designed to cut out new materialThe system’s appeal was that it could reduce the amount of material moved for road construction. With the traditional method, crews would have to mill and haul away the pavement, then bring new material to the construction site. This system was designed to carry out those steps continuously on site. Fast Company also noted that in October 2019, the city of Los Angeles wanted to conduct tests on two different areas of road in December. The duration of the trial run would be one to two years.The environmental benefit also depended on the process temperature. Unlike traditional hot-mix asphalt paving, the technology worked at normal temperatures and avoided transporting both the old material and the replacement material. The company projected that the process would greatly reduce emissions, but these figures were estimates rather than measurements from the completed roadway. Los Angeles had also been increasing its use of reclaimed asphalt pavement, with Asphalt Plant No. 1 expected to raise the share of recycled asphalt pavement in its hot-mix asphalt from 20% to 50%. This broader effort provided context for the trial, as the city was exploring ways to keep more pavement material in use rather than sending it to waste.Testing plastic roads in the real worldThe idea attracted attention partly because the company said laboratory tests suggest plastic-based roads could last eight to 13 times longer than conventional asphalt. Research published in the Journal of Traffic and Transportation Engineering similarly shows that recycled plastics can influence asphalt's mechanical and thermal properties, but stresses that compatibility, storage stability, processing methods and long-term performance remain important considerations.This trial mattered because it was a real-world application, though it did not prove that plastic roads could replace conventional roads everywhere. It aimed to combine recycled PET and asphalt in a way that reduced the amount of binder needed and cut transportation of materials. It also suggested a model in which road repairs become a recycling process, with the old road forming much of the new one.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Psychology says children who sing while getting dressed, eating or playing may be doing more than just having fun
articles.summary: Some children turn almost anything into a song. Getting dressed becomes a little tune. A trip to the supermarket gets its own lyrics.
articles.body: Some children turn almost anything into a song. Getting dressed becomes a little tune. A trip to the supermarket gets its own lyrics. They sing about what they are eating, what they are doing, who is coming home and even what happened five minutes ago. The songs may make little sense to an adult. The same line may be repeated again and again, sometimes with a made-up melody and sometimes with just a rhythmic chant. But spontaneous singing is a common part of young children's everyday lives. Research suggests that children can use singing not only for entertainment but also as a way to communicate, play with language, repeat ideas and take control of everyday situations.Why do children turn ordinary moments into songs?Young children often sing while they are already doing something else, playing, getting dressed, eating or moving around the house. A naturalistic study that recorded 15 three and four-year-old children during their normal routines at home found that spontaneous singing occurred in everyday situations and could take different forms, including invented or improvised songs. The important point is that these songs are not necessarily something an adult has taught the child. Children can invent lyrics, repeat familiar patterns and change songs as they go.Repetition gives the child a structureListen closely to a child's made-up song and one thing often stands out: repetition. The same words may appear several times. A child's name may be repeated. An action may be turned into a chorus. Sometimes the melody stays the same while the words change. That repetition can make an ordinary sequence easier to follow and remember. Research on children's song learning has found that young children can encode words and tunes in memory, showing that song provides a structured way for verbal information to be represented and remembered. A 2022 study involving preschool children also found that teaching words through songs or rhythmically spoken songs produced greater gains in the depth of word knowledge than teaching the same words through picture cards alone. This does not mean that singing every instruction will automatically improve a child's memory. But rhythm, repetition and words presented together can give children another way to engage with language.Sometimes the child is singing to themselvesThere is another interesting pattern: children do not always sing for an audience. They may sing quietly while playing alone or working on something. A study of 58 children aged 4 to 8 examined private speech, singing and humming during tasks involving attention and executive functioning. Nearly one-third of the children used private song, while almost all used some form of private speech. The researchers found that private singing itself was not associated with executive-function performance, so the study does not show that singing makes children better at self-control. But it does show that private singing is something children spontaneously use while engaging with tasks.Songs can help children take part in everyday routinesAdults often use songs to make routines easier for young children. Children can also create their own versions. Research involving multilingual toddlers in preschool found that singing activities provided children with lyrics, gestures, rhythm and repetition, creating different ways to participate in communication and group activities. This may help explain why children sometimes create songs around routines that happen every day. A repeated tune can become part of the routine itself.Making up songs is also a form of creativityThere is another side to spontaneous singing that is easy to miss. Children are not simply repeating songs they have heard. They can invent lyrics, change melodies and create songs around whatever is happening at that moment. A study examining children's early music-making found that invented songs could show children's capacity for musical elaboration and creative activity. The researchers followed young children's song-making and looked at how their musical ideas developed in everyday contexts. A child singing “Papa is making tea, Papa is making tea, where is my biscuit?” may not be trying to create a meaningful piece of music. They may simply be playing with words and sounds. But that play itself is part of how young children experiment with language and musical ideas.What parents should not assumeA child who suddenly starts singing about school, friends or a particular event is not necessarily revealing a hidden worry. Children sing about things because they are interested in them. They repeat words because repetition is enjoyable. They change lyrics because making things up is fun. Parents do not need to analyse every song for a deeper meaning. Instead, it can be useful to listen to the pattern. Is the child repeating certain words? Are they changing the ending each time? Are they making up a tune for a routine they usually find boring? Are they singing alone while concentrating on something? These details can tell parents more about how the child is using the song.Let the child keep making up the rulesIf a child turns breakfast into a song, there is no need to correct the lyrics. Parents can join in, add a line or simply ask, “What comes next?” They can also encourage the child to make songs about ordinary activities, getting ready for school, putting toys away or remembering the steps of a task without turning it into a formal lesson. The value may not be in whether the song is “good”. It may be in the child's freedom to repeat, change, remember and rearrange words and sounds.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Nashville replaced 6.5 acres of parking with Cumberland Park; a hidden tank beneath it now captures about 1 million gallons of stormwater from nearby streets each year
articles.summary: Discover how Nashville transformed a 6.5-acre parking lot into Cumberland Park, an innovative green space that captures and reuses 1 million gallons of stormwater each year, promoting environmental sustainability.
articles.body: A large paved parking area is not usually thought of as part of a city's water infrastructure. In Nashville, Tennessee, however, a former parking site along the Cumberland River was transformed into Cumberland Park, a 6.5-acre public space designed to combine recreation with measures for managing rainwater.According to City Parks Alliance, Cumberland Park opened in 2012 as part of Nashville's wider riverfront redevelopment. Beneath the landscaped park is a rainwater-harvesting cistern that captures stormwater from the park, nearby streets and parking areas. The system can collect about 1 million gallons of water in a typical year, which is then reused to irrigate the park.From parking lot to public parkCumberland Park sits on the east bank of the Cumberland River, beneath the Shelby Street Bridge, on a 6.5-acre site that was once largely occupied by surface parking and other developed land. The redevelopment turned the area into a public landscape with lawns, walking paths, play areas, gardens, a climbing wall and an outdoor amphitheatre. The project formed part of Nashville's New Riverfront Revitalisation Plan, which aimed to reconnect downtown with the river, while its design also had to account for the area's floodplain. The 2010 Nashville floods, when the Cumberland River reached levels not seen since the 1930s, led designers to reconsider parts of the project before construction was completed. According to the Tennessee Department of Environment and Conservation, the redevelopment also included brownfield remediation, floodplain preservation and habitat restoration, with more than 1.6 acres of meadow and riparian grasses restored as part of the project.Water hidden beneath the landscapeAmong other features of Cumberland Park is the stormwater management system. According to the City Parks Alliance, there is also an underground cistern which is able to collect around 1 million gallons of stormwater annually. In addition, this water is not discharged to the municipal stormwater system but is used for irrigation purposes. Initially, the design of the project explained the system of collecting the stormwater from the park, as well as the parking lot and adjacent vehicle bridge.This is one instance where a city park does more than just offer empty spaces. In this park, rainwater is not drained away but instead stored in the ground and then used at a later time. This is especially significant in a place like Nashville, where heavy rainfall leads to large amounts of surface runoff. In this city, the stormwater system typically moves rainwater through the drains, pipes and ditches into creeks and rivers. The runoff from the streets might even have pollutants mixed in.A park with several jobsManaging stormwater runoff was only a portion of the redevelopment of Cumberland Park. It was also hoped that Cumberland Park would provide new green space along a portion of the riverfront area where there was previously a predominance of paving and industry. There is an amphitheatre at Cumberland Park that can hold up to 1,200 individuals, as well as water-play elements, paths, and areas for recreation. In addition, native and traditional planting was included in the landscaping of the site, and meadow and riparian restoration added plants to the riverfront area.Contaminants found during the assessment process included Polycyclic Aromatic Hydrocarbons, Lead, and Arsenic in various sections of the former brownfield. It included processes such as soil excavation, capping of certain sites and institutional controls before the land could be put back into use as a public park. Therefore, the water collection process is part of a bigger redevelopment project. The former parking lot has been transformed to become public space, the contaminated land has been remediated, vegetation planted, and rainwater harvested.The Cumberland Park project demonstrates how one piece of urban land can be used in more than one way. On the surface level, the park is an area where people can walk, play, and meet by the river. Beneath the surface, the infrastructure is able to store rainwater. Once impervious and paved, the land has been redeveloped to catch and reuse some of the rainwater.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: In 2014, a woman left Oregon alone to walk the world; after six and a half years, she returned with 20,000 miles and one terrifying attack behind her
articles.summary: In 2014, Angela Maxwell embarked on a six-and-a-half-year journey, walking around the world solo, overcoming challenges like heat stroke, dengue fever, and a terrifying assault. Discover her inspiring story of resilience, self-discovery, and adventure.
articles.body: On 2 May 2014, Angela Maxwell left Bend, Oregon, with a two-wheeled cart, camping equipment and no fixed end date. She had decided to walk around the world, despite having little previous experience with long-distance hiking. What began as an unusual personal challenge eventually became a six-and-a-half-year journey across four continents, 14 countries and more than 20,000 miles.According to ABC News, Maxwell had been working as a life coach and business consultant when she began thinking about making a major change. She had heard about people who had travelled around the world on foot and became fascinated by the idea. Within about nine months, she had sold most of her belongings, prepared her equipment and set off. Her journey was not a continuous walk the entire way. She used flights between some destinations and walked for long stretches once she arrived.A journey planned one leg at a timeMaxwell's preparation was relatively short for an expedition of such scale. She told ABC that she had no previous hiking experience and spent about nine months researching equipment, reading about women adventurers and building up her fitness. She eventually carried her belongings in a two-wheeled cart, which became a familiar part of her journey. She spent about $5 a day, which meant camping much of the time and carrying her own food and water. Her meals were often simple, including oatmeal and instant noodles. The cart held her tent, cooking equipment, clothing and other supplies, allowing her to remain largely self-sufficient while travelling.Her route changed as she travelled. She walked from Bend to Portland, then flew to Western Australia and travelled north through some of the country's harshest terrain. She later continued through New Zealand, Southeast Asia, Mongolia and Europe. Her route later took her through Italy, Georgia, Turkey, Switzerland, France, Belgium, England and Scotland before she returned to the United States. The physical demands were considerable. In Australia, she experienced heat stroke and severe sun blisters. In Vietnam, she contracted dengue fever and spent about a month recovering. Yet Maxwell has said that the walking itself was not always the hardest part. Being alone and deciding whether it was safe to continue often required more from her than the distance did.The night in MongoliaAccording to BBC Travel, about a year into her journey, Maxwell experienced one of its most frightening moments in Mongolia when a nomad broke into her tent and sexually assaulted her. After the attack, she moved away from the campsite and spent the remaining hours of darkness hiding with her cart before deciding what to do next. Despite the experience, Maxwell continued her journey and eventually completed her walk around the world.It was the only time during the expedition when she seriously thought about giving up on the trip. Maxwell went on to say that thinking about stories of other women who had managed to survive an attack inspired her to keep going. This experience made her rethink how she approached her safety. Throughout the rest of the trip, she was more vigilant at night, especially when camping out, and she took further steps to protect herself in her tent. She chose to include this experience in her story, but it did not define the entire trip. Most of Maxwell's experiences were with people who helped her on her journey.Six and a half years laterMaxwell reached her destination on December 16, 2020, and returned to Bend, where her journey had begun, to the home of the friend who had helped her set out on the adventure. By then, she had covered more than 20,000 miles and spent six and a half years travelling from one country to another and from one landscape to another. Finishing the trip was not easy. Later, Maxwell said she had changed after years without belongings, talking to strangers and living with uncertainty. When she returned, walking had taken on a different meaning: an attempt to lead a life based on simplicity, travelling slowly and figuring out how far she could go on her own.You use AI every day. articles.title: Amrinder Singh Raja Warring changes X bio after stepping down as Punjab Congress chief
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Congress leader Amrinder Singh Raja Warring on Thursday changed his X bio to \"former Punjab Pradesh Congress Committee President\" amid
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Congress leader Amrinder Singh Raja Warring on Thursday changed his X bio to "former Punjab Pradesh Congress Committee President" amid speculation that the Congress high command has asked the Ludhiana MP to step down from the top party post in the state amid a factional feud.This comes hours after Warring declined to comment on reports that the party high command had decided to replace him, saying that “some issues are internal”.The move comes after months of infighting within the Punjab Congress, which intensified after the party high command decided on July 1 to retain Warring as the state unit chief.A section of leaders led by former chief minister Charanjit Singh Channi had opposed Warring’s continuation and sought his removal. Leaders aligned with the Channi camp also stayed away from party programmes led by Warring.According to PTI, the Congress general secretary and Punjab in-charge held a series of meetings with state leaders before submitting his report to the party high command on the proposed leadership change.The high command subsequently informed Warring of its decision, party sources told PTI, adding that the Congress is now looking to appoint a leader who can bring different factions together ahead of the 2027 assembly polls.Former minister and ex-MP Vijay Inder Singla has emerged as a frontrunner for the post, sources said. The other names being discussed include former Olympian and Jalandhar Cantt MLA Pargat Singh, former MLA Rana KP Singh, Raja Sansi MLA Sukhbinder Singh Sarkaria, former chief minister Charanjit Singh Channi and Gurdaspur MP Sukhjinder Singh Randhawa.The leadership tussle has played out publicly in recent months, raising concerns within the party over its impact on the Congress campaign as it seeks to return to power in Punjab.The factionalism has also added to concerns over the party’s ability to consolidate its organisation ahead of the assembly polls.Asked about the possibility of a change in the Punjab Congress leadership on Tuesday, Channi said the decision was the prerogative of the party high command.“It is the prerogative of Rahul Gandhi and (Mallikarjun) Kharge ji. Only they know who is to be appointed or when is to be changed,” Channi told reporters in Delhi.Warring had also faced criticism from sections of the party over the Congress’ electoral performance in Punjab and his leadership.In August, he defended himself against criticism over the party’s decline in the 2022 assembly elections, questioning attempts to hold him responsible for the loss.“The only mistake is that when the Congress Party had 80 seats, we came down from 80 to 18 seats. Is that my fault? Captain Amarinder Singh led the government twice. From 80 seats, we came down to 18 seats,” he had said.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Jersey old age pension tops £16,000 a year after 4.7% increase
articles.summary: The full pension rises by £734 a year, or about £14 a week, the Government of Jersey says.
articles.body:
Jersey pensioners are to receive an increase of £734 a year to their old age pension as a top-up comes into effect.

The Government of Jersey said the 4.7% increase, an additional £14 per week for someone on a full pension, would bring the overall sum to £16,294 per year.

The pension is updated every October by at least the recorded increase in the pensioner retail price index for June.

Minister for Social Security Senator Elaine Millar said further support, including cold weather payments and free TV licences, would be available for those on low incomes.

Deputy Millar said: "Our pensioners have contributed to Jersey throughout their working lives and it is important that the old age pension continues to provide a strong foundation for old age.

"We also recognise that pensioners on lower incomes can face particular pressure from healthcare and heating costs, which is why additional support is available through Pension Plus, the Health Access Scheme and the Cold Weather Bonus."

Millar said she encouraged anyone who believed they could be eligible for extra help to "check what support is available to them".

The social security minister said last month it was a priority for her to introduce mandatory workplace pensions alongside the government pension.

articles.title: At 7, Arizona girl Sloan started collecting diapers after seeing a Phoenix food bank run out; five years later, the 12-year-old aimed for 22,500 and delivered 30,000 diapers in her fifth annual drive
articles.summary: Recently, Nourish Phoenix, a food bank in Phoenix, received its largest diaper donation ever.
articles.body: Recently, Nourish Phoenix, a food bank in Phoenix, received its largest diaper donation ever. A U-Haul filled with diapers for families across the community arrived at the food bank, leaving the employees shocked to learn that not some philanthropic millionaire, but a middle-schooler was behind the enormous load.While most children her age live life blissfully ignorant of the world's problems, 12-year-old Sloan spends her time collecting diapers. This time, she sent a package of 30,000 to the food bank. This year, her target was 22,500 diapers for donation, but the Huggies, Pampers and Blueys kept pouring in until there was hardly any room to walk around her home.According to research from the National Diaper Bank Network and Huggies, roughly 1 in 3 US families struggle to afford enough diapers to keep their baby clean, dry and healthy. With diapers not being covered by SNAP or WIC, families end up spending more on them. For many families visiting the food bank, every dollar matters and diapers can quickly become the most expensive product to spend on.Interestingly, this wasn't Sloan's first donation drive. It was her fifth annual 'Diaper Drive', an event she has been organising since the age of seven, all the while volunteering at the food bank.Nourish Phoenix has been helping families in Phoenix with food, clothing, hygiene products and job assistance since the 1960s. It was in 2022 that she visited the food bank alongside her mother to help prepare food boxes for the families to pick up. Afterwards, the team gave her a tour of the facility and Sloan noticed a section of shelves at the food bank's location at 510 on 9th Avenue was bare. When she questioned the empty space, she was told that it was where the diapers were, that they were always among the most requested items, and yet had already run out. On the way home, Sloan said, "Mom, we should get some diapers and bring them back for Nourish Phoenix."After seeing the need firsthand, she launched her first diaper drive through a social media post, collecting about 7,000 diapers. Five years later, her annual effort has grown into a community-wide movement fueled by donations from family, friends and supporters through Sloan's Diaper Drive.“If we have the ability to give someone something that they might not have or need, it’s really important to do that,” she said in an interview with ABC 15 as her diaper drive concluded at the close of August“My little girl: she’s just so special, she has such a big heart, loves helping and giving back,” said Sloan’s proud mother.You use AI every day. articles.title: 'We've been without internet for nearly a month'
articles.summary: Frensham residents say they found it "very scary" after their broadband suddenly stopped working.
articles.body:
Residents of a Surrey village have expressed anger after they were hit by a prolonged broadband outage.

Jill, from Frensham, said it was "very scary" when the internet "suddenly disappeared" on 5 September as her husband's heart monitor needs connectivity.

"The most important thing for me is to make sure that the hospital knows what's happening with his body so they can keep an eye on him," she said.

An Openreach spokesperson has apologised for the loss of service, which it blamed on a burst water pipe damaging underground cables.

They added on Thursday morning that repairs had been completed and villagers should have their broadband restored.

Vicky Kenish, another Frensham resident, said she has been "terribly, terribly stressed" since losing internet.

"I've got to the state where I can't even think about it," she told BBC Radio Surrey .

Living in an area with poor mobile data, Kenish said the lack of broadband had caused many problems, such as she could not look at bus times when her car broke.

"Everything we do nowadays we need internet for," she said. "When suddenly it's disappearing, it's really scary."

Her landline was also not functioning, Kenish continued.

She added Openreach said multiple times the connection would be restored, though it was not.

How 'abandoned' locals installed their own broadband

Mark Billings, from Frensham, said he has also been without internet for over three weeks.

Most devices in his house were linked to WiFi, such as light switches, which had not been working properly, he added.

"The key point is that we have never got any information from them [Openreach]," he told the BBC.

Openreach said: "We would like to thank customers for their patience....and we apologise for the disruption this incident has caused."

articles.title: Why humans fell for coffee: The history, chemistry and science behind every cup
articles.summary: Relationships in modern life are quite unpredictable.
articles.body: Relationships in modern life are quite unpredictable. Friends reschedule, bosses send late-night emails, plans change at a moment’s notice, and even the most carefully constructed routines can be disrupted by an unexpected call or a delayed commute.But there is one relationship in our lives that is remarkably dependable. It asks very little in return and offers a small, reliable dose of comfort almost every morning: our coffee. And today, we will discuss how the most dependable relationship of our times is our silent, comforting and unbreakable bond with the cuppa containing coffee.Because today is International Coffee Day – a day where the world celebrates the journey of coffee from bean to cup while supporting millions of farmers and advocating for fair trade and sustainability.In an increasingly chaotic world, the morning cuppa has evolved into something much more than a quick shot of caffeine to kickstart the day. It has become a fiercely protected ritual, a pocket of familiarity and, for many of us, one of the few things we can still control.We know exactly how it should taste, which mug we want to drink it from, where we want to sit while drinking it and, most importantly, when we want to be left alone with it.The coffee itself may take only a few minutes to make, but the ritual around it can hold an entire morning together.How we fell in love: A quick historyWe didn’t build this deep bond overnight. Coffee has travelled a long way from being something consumed primarily for its stimulating effect to becoming a lifestyle, a social experience and finally, for many people, a deeply personal ritual.The early history of modern coffee culture was largely utilitarian though. Coffee was something that helped people wake up, work longer and get through the day. Instant coffee and canned grounds made preparation quick and convenient, and the emphasis was less on the experience of making or drinking coffee than on what it could do for you. It was, quite literally, fuel.Then came the coffee shop boom of the late twentieth century, and coffee began to acquire a different meaning. Cafés turned the drink into a social experience. We learned the vocabulary of espresso, cappuccino, latte and mocha, developed preferences about milk and sugar, and began meeting friends, colleagues and dates over coffee. Coffee shops became places to linger rather than merely places to consume a beverage.Coffee also became a lifestyle marker. The cup in your hand could say something about you: what you liked, where you went, what kind of neighbourhood you belonged to, even how you wanted to be perceived. The humble cup of coffee had acquired a social life of its own.Today, that relationship has taken a more intimate turn. We have brought the coffee shop into our kitchens. Armed with whole-bean grinders, pour-over equipment, French presses, Aeropresses and carefully-chosen beans, we have turned brewing into a quiet personal craft. Water temperature matters. Grind size matters. The origin of the bean matters. Even the shape of the mug matters.The heartbeat of coffee culture has, in some ways, moved from the noisy commercial café back into the home. And that has laid the groundwork for the personal morning rituals we protect today.Coffee has moved from fuel, to social experience, to personal ritual.That evolution explains why the first cup of the day can feel strangely important even when the drink itself is relatively ordinary. Or, is it?The science of the morning ritualWhy does such a simple routine mean so much to us? There is an important distinction between a habit and a ritual. A habit is something we do almost automatically because we have done it so many times before. A ritual involves greater attention and intention. The steps may be familiar, but we attach meaning to them.A 2018 Northwestern University study offers an interesting clue as to why coffee became the morning ritual all over the world. Researchers found that people who were more sensitive to the bitter taste of caffeine actually tended to drink more coffee. One possible reason, they suggested, is that we learn to associate that bitterness with the alertness and energy that follows. In other words, we may come to like coffee not despite its bitterness, but because our brain has learned what that bitterness promises.Plus, making coffee is a ritual for us because it engages so many senses and involves a sequence we have consciously created. Measuring the beans, grinding them, hearing the machine come to life, watching hot water move through the coffee, smelling the aroma and finally taking that first sip all turn a mundane activity into a small sensory experience.And when life outside that ritual feels unpredictable, predictability can itself be comforting.There is a reason people become very particular about their morning coffee. It is not necessarily being fussy. It is often about familiarity. We know what we are going to get. We know what the first sip will taste like. We know where we will sit and how long we have before the rest of the day begins.Psychological research on rituals has suggested that performing meaningful, structured routines can help people feel a greater sense of control, particularly when circumstances around them feel uncertain. The ritual does not magically make the problem disappear. What it can do is create a brief moment in which the person feels grounded enough to face it.This may explain why the coffee ritual becomes especially precious during periods of stress. When work is chaotic, when the news is overwhelming or when the day ahead feels difficult to predict, there is something reassuring about doing the same small thing in the same familiar way.And there is another curious element to this: slowing down can change the way we experience the coffee itself.When we pay attention to what we are drinking rather than swallowing it while scrolling through emails, the sensory experience becomes richer. We notice the aroma, temperature, texture and aftertaste. The coffee may not actually have changed, but our experience of it has.The ritual, in other words, can make us better at experiencing the thing we are consuming.It’s all in your mind — and your favourite mugScientists studying sensory perception have long established that flavour is not simply a property of food or drink. It is constructed by the brain using information from several senses at once.That helps explain why the same coffee can feel different depending on where, how and from what we drink it.Take the mug. Most of us have one. Or many. Our favourite one may be chipped, oversized, inherited from someone or completely unremarkable to anyone else, but somehow it is our mug. We reach for it without thinking.Research into cross-modal perception—the ability of the brain to interact, exchange, and combine information from two or more different sensory systems—suggests that the physical characteristics of a vessel can influence how we perceive what is inside it.For instance, a heavier cup can contribute to an expectation of a more substantial or premium experience. Colour can influence expectations about flavour too, with different colours being associated with qualities such as sweetness, bitterness or intensity.Then there is sound. The environment in which we drink coffee can affect how we experience its flavour. Loud background noise can interfere with the perception of certain tastes, while a quieter environment allows us to pay greater attention to aroma and flavour.This is why the perfect cup is rarely just about the coffee. It is the mug. It is the chair. It is the light coming through the window. It is the smell of toast in the kitchen, the newspaper on the table or the playlist you have been listening to for years. It is the first few minutes before the phone starts buzzing.The coffee becomes a kind of sensory shorthand for all those things. Which is perhaps why spilling coffee on your shirt at 8.30am can feel like much more than spilling coffee.The protected 10 minutesThink about your ideal morning. It may involve a favourite worn mug, a particular roast, your balcony, a kitchen counter or a corner chair where you like to sit. Perhaps, there is a newspaper, a book or a playlist. Perhaps, you simply stare out of the window and do absolutely nothing.The details are different for everyone, but the underlying idea is remarkably similar: these few minutes belong to you.That is what has become most valuable. Because modern life is filled with interruptions. Notifications begin before breakfast. Work messages arrive on phones that were once meant to connect us only to other people. Meetings stretch across time zones. Social media delivers an endless stream of other people's lives. Even leisure time can feel crowded with things we are expected to watch, read, respond to or keep up with.Against that backdrop, a simple coffee ritual can feel almost rebellious. For 10 minutes, you decide the pace. It is a tiny form of control in a life that often offers very little of it.This is why people can become surprisingly protective of their coffee time. Interrupt someone during their morning coffee and you may discover just how emotionally invested they are in those few minutes. It is not the caffeine they are defending. It is the space around it.There is something comforting about having one small part of the day that remains almost exactly as you expect it to be. The world may have changed overnight. Your inbox may be overflowing. Your schedule may already be running late. But the coffee is there, familiar and reassuring, waiting in the same mug.Of course, coffee is not a substitute for human relationships. It cannot listen to your problems, remember your birthday or tell you that everything is going to be fine. But it can occupy a peculiar emotional space in our lives because it asks so little of us. We don’t have to explain ourselves to our cuppa. We don't have to be interesting, productive or available. We simply have to sit down and drink it.The relationship is wonderfully uncomplicated. We know what to expect from it, we can personalise it endlessly and, unlike most modern relationships, it rarely sends a confusing message at midnight.That’s why the morning cup has become a daily reset button – a sensory pleasure and a small declaration that before the demands of the day begin, there will be a few minutes that belong entirely to us.So yes, we drink coffee for the caffeine. We drink it because we like the taste, because we need to wake up, because someone has invited us for a coffee or because the café makes an excellent latte.But mostly, we are drinking it for familiarity. For ritual. For the comfort of repetition. For 10 quiet minutes before the world comes rushing in.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.body: Every year on October 2, the country pauses to remember Mahatma Gandhi, the man whose quiet, unshakeable belief in truth and non-violence somehow managed to shake an empire loose from its grip on India. Gandhi Jayanti isn't just a public holiday marked with a day off work, it's meant to be a moment of genuine reflection, a chance to think about what those values, honesty, restraint, compassion, actually look like in ordinary, everyday life rather than just in history textbooks. Whether you're sending a message to family, posting something thoughtful for friends to see, or just want the right words for a WhatsApp status this year, here's a solid collection of wishes, quotes, and messages to mark the occasion meaningfully.Why Gandhi Jayanti still matters todayIt's easy, especially for younger generations who never lived through the freedom struggle, to see Gandhi Jayanti as just another date on the calendar. But the ideals Gandhi stood for, non-violence, self-discipline, standing firm in truth even when it's inconvenient, remain genuinely relevant well beyond the context of colonial India. In a world that often rewards loud, aggressive posturing, Gandhi's insistence that real strength lies in restraint and moral clarity feels almost radical again. That's really the spirit worth carrying into whatever message you choose to send this year, not just nostalgia, but an actual nod to values still worth practising.Heartfelt wishes to send this Gandhi Jayanti"On this Gandhi Jayanti, let's remember that true strength lies not in force, but in truth and compassion. Wishing you a thoughtful and peaceful day.""May the ideals of the Father of the Nation continue to guide us toward a kinder, more honest world. Happy Gandhi Jayanti.""Gandhi taught us that even the smallest act of kindness carries weight. Sending you warm wishes on this meaningful day.""On this special day, let's pledge to carry forward Bapu's message of peace, simplicity, and truth in our own small ways. Happy Gandhi Jayanti.""May this Gandhi Jayanti inspire all of us to choose patience over anger and understanding over conflict. Wishing you a reflective day."Messages worth sharing with family and friends"Bapu once said the best way to find yourself is to lose yourself in the service of others. Let's honour that today by being a little kinder to those around us.""This Gandhi Jayanti, let's remember that freedom isn't just something we inherited, it's something we're responsible for protecting through how we live each day.""A day to remember the man who proved that quiet resolve can achieve what force never could. Happy Gandhi Jayanti to you and your family.""On Bapu's birth anniversary, let's take a moment to reflect on truth, non-violence, and the kind of world we're building for the next generation.""May this day remind us that real change often starts with the smallest, most personal choices we make. Wishing you a peaceful Gandhi Jayanti."Gandhi's own words, worth revisiting every yearGandhi's own writings and speeches remain some of the most quoted lines in Indian history, and revisiting a few of them each year tends to hit differently depending on where you are in life. Among his most enduring lines is the reminder that you must become the change you wish to see in the world, a phrase so widely repeated it's almost become shorthand for the man himself. He also famously said that honesty is more a matter of courage than of intelligence, something worth reflecting on in a world that often confuses cleverness with integrity. Another of his often-cited thoughts is that the weak can never forgive, since forgiveness itself is an attribute reserved for the strong.Facebook captions for the occasion"Remembering the Father of the Nation today, and everything he taught us about courage without violence. #GandhiJayanti2026""Truth, simplicity, and non-violence, values worth carrying well beyond just today. Happy Gandhi Jayanti to everyone.""A tribute to Bapu, whose life proved that principles matter more than power. #Bapu #GandhiJayanti""On this day, let's honour Gandhi not just with words, but with a little more patience and kindness in how we treat each other."WhatsApp status ideas that actually say something"Be the change. Always. #GandhiJayanti""Truth and non-violence, simple words, harder to live by than most of us admit.""Remembering Bapu today, and the quiet power of standing firm without raising a fist.""Gandhi Jayanti: a reminder that real strength doesn't shout."Making the day mean something beyond a messageSending a wish or posting a quote is a nice gesture, but a lot of people also choose to mark Gandhi Jayanti with something a little more active, volunteering for a cleanliness drive, since the day also coincides with the Swachh Bharat Abhiyan's anniversary, or simply spending time discussing what Gandhi's principles might look like applied to modern problems, from social media outrage to everyday conflict resolution. Schools and offices often organise small readings or discussions around his life, and joining even a brief one can make the day feel a little less like a formality and a little more like genuine reflection.A day to pause, even brieflyWhatever combination of wishes, quotes, or messages you end up sending this year, the real point of Gandhi Jayanti is the pause it asks for, a small break from the noise of everyday life to think about restraint, honesty, and the kind of world worth building through ordinary, daily choices. It doesn't need to be a grand gesture. Sometimes just sending a thoughtful message to someone, and actually meaning it, is enough to keep Gandhi's ideals quietly alive for one more year.Get the latest movie news, reviews, and celebrity updates. articles.title: Captain Smit Machchhar: The ‘jovial’ pilot and father who thwarted the Flydubai attacker
articles.summary: The Indian pilot who fought off a savage attack by his copilot and helped prevent an apparent hijack of a Flydubai plane heading to Israel with more than 170...
articles.body:
The Indian pilot who fought off a savage attack by his copilot and helped prevent an apparent hijack of a Flydubai plane heading to Israel with more than 170 people on board is being hailed as a hero.

Captain Smit Machchhar was stabbed while trying to fend off the attacker, leaving him badly wounded. During the struggle the cockpit door was opened, allowing other passengers to rush in, subdue his assailant, and take control of the plane that was enroute to Tel Aviv.

Machchhar's actions have received widespread praise from political leaders, passengers who were onboard, those who know him as well as strangers who gathered in his home town to celebrate his bravery.

Kaushik Gandhi, who lives in the same building as Machchhar's parents, told CNN the pilot was always smiling and happy, a real "gentleman."

He described Machchhar as "first class" and said he would always say hello when visiting.

"Our entire India should be proud … he has brought glory to India's name everywhere in the world," Gandhi told CNN, adding he was "thumping (his) chest" in pride.

A crowd of supporters have also gathered in Ghatkopar East, the eastern Mumbai suburb where Machchhar's family lives. They were waving Indian flags and photos of the hero pilot.

"It is a very precious moment and proud moment for a country like us that we have been through, you know, lot of hustles," Rahul Pandey, one of those gathered there, told CNN.

"Smit Machchhar is a talented, soft spoken, kind-hearted and a person with good nature," said Jinat Shah, who used to live next door to him in Mumbai before the pilot moved to Dubai. "He is an incredible person, and I hope for his fast recovery," Shah told Indian news agency ANI.

Passengers who were on flight FZ1073 described those chaotic moments , during which the plane plummeted 17,400 feet in less than 120 seconds. One told CNN: "I was just sure I was going to die."

But after the attacker was restrained, the flight was diverted to Saudi Arabia, where it was safely landed by two standby pilots who happened to be flying as passengers

Machchhar, who is reported to be a 39-year-old father of two, was seriously wounded in the attack.

Images show showed a gruesome scene onboard following the attack, with blood splashed across the cockpit and the seriously wounded pilot lying on the floor, his pained face partially covered with a mask.

Machchhar had suffered "massive blood loss" and was "severely wounded," dentist Shota Musaev, a passenger on the flight who helped treat him, told CNN.

"I think that if we had waited even a few more moments, we would have lost him; his blood pressure had plummeted, he suddenly lost consciousness, and there was blood everywhere," he said.

His bravery "managed to prevent a 9/11 disaster," Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu told CNN.

Machchhar is receiving medical care at a hospital in Saudi Arabia, according to the Indian embassy in Riyadh, and is in stable condition.

Parag Shah, who represents Ghatkopar East, the eastern Mumbai suburb Machchhar is from, told CNN that the pilot was "out of danger" after undergoing surgery on Wednesday, citing family members.

Born into a family in the textile business, becoming a pilot wasn't Machchhar's "childhood dream," he told the Bona-Fide Banter podcast in 2025.

Initially, he'd enrolled in a textile engineering course after school.

"I finished the entire course, I still was young so wanted to (do) a little more studies," he said.

Once he decided on flying, training took him to New Zealand, where he arrived aged around 19, in the southern city of Dunedin.

"He was always sort of a jovial young man and he tried hard," his instructor at the time Philip Kean told CNN.

In a group photograph Kean shared from those days, Machchhar is easy to pick out. "He definitely got a smile of his own… he's sort of a happy, happy chap," said Kean, CEO of Mainland Air in Dunedin.

Before joining Flydubai, Machchhar spent 11 years with Indian carrier SpiceJet, rising to the position of Senior Commander, according to his LinkedIn profile.

Before Wednesday's incident, one of the most unusual situations he had faced during his over 15 years of flying was the birth of a baby on board.

A woman on the plane, who was not at term, had started experiencing labor pains, Machchhar told the Bona-Fide Banter podcast. "Within 7-10 minutes, she was like, 'captain this is now advancing toward a delivery.'"

Machchhar said he and the first officer started to check for the nearest airfields and conditions to make a safe landing. "Both the mother baby were fine," he added.

Watching the news of Machchhar's heroic actions on the Flydubai flight from New Zealand, his former instructor Kean was full of praise for the young man he had once taught.

"There could have been a whole airplane load of people wiped out in a matter of seconds, and luckily they got the door open… luckily he could hang on and save the day. Another half a minute would have been all over."

"I'm very proud," he said. "I'm very proud that he handled that situation… It's great the way it turned out."

Machchhar has become a national hero for two nations –– Israel, where most of the passengers hailed from, and his own home country, India.

"The pilot from Mumbai who proved to be a hero," wrote the Times of India.

"Viewers, if 166 Israelis go home tonight without a scratch, it is all down to the bravery of one single Indian, Captain Smit Machchhar," a CNN News-18 anchor said during his primetime program.

Speaking on the podcast last year how he felt to be a pilot, Machchhar's answer was simple: "Blessed."

articles.title: Himachal implements mandatory dress code for teachers in government CBSE schools
articles.summary: Himachal Pradesh implemented a mandatory dress code for teachers across 148 government CBSE schools on Thursday, attempting to create a more organised and
articles.body: Himachal Pradesh implemented a mandatory dress code for teachers across 148 government CBSE schools on Thursday, attempting to create a more organised and professional learning environment.A notice dated September 10 explained that the prescribed dress code has been formulated "keeping in view the professional requirements of the teaching profession, uniformity in appearance and the climatic conditions of Himachal Pradesh."The dress code's colour palette includes light lilac, lilac purple and navy blue, with black prescribed for footwear and other specified accessories.The prescribed dress code offers female teachers three alternatives: a saree with a blazer, a kurta/kameez with pants, a plazo or salwar and a blazer, and a shirt and blazer with pants and a tie. For male teachers, however, only a single formal combination has been laid down: shirt with a tie, pants, and a blazer.According to the notice, the dress code is mandatory and will apply to all teachers, including principals, without exception, regardless of how they were recruited or engaged. This includes teachers whose services are being availed on an outsourced basis, for the time being.Reasonable adjustments may be allowed with the approval of the head of the institution in cases of medical necessity, disability or pregnancy.The state government also plans to open 100 new CBSE schools from the coming academic session, while roughly 2,000 teaching posts in CBSE schools have already been filled, PTI reported.To reinforce accountability, a system that logs teachers' attendance three times a day is also being brought in.Director of school education, Ashish Kohli, said the reforms had made a positive difference to the education sector, placing greater importance on quality education, equal opportunities, accountability and learning centred on students. He added that this had made Himachal Pradesh a role model for education reforms.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.
