articles.title: Trouble ahead of midterm elections? Americans are turning against Donald Trump's handling of economy, prices
articles.summary: Americans are increasingly unhappy with President Donald Trump’s handling of the economy and rising prices, with a new poll showing a sharp drop in his
articles.body: Americans are increasingly unhappy with President Donald Trump’s handling of the economy and rising prices, with a new poll showing a sharp drop in his economic approval and a majority blaming his policies for persistently high costs.Only 17% of US adults approve of Trump’s handling of the cost of living, while just 26% approve of his handling of the economy, according to an Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research poll.The economic approval figure is a new low and is down 14 percentage points from March 2025, shortly after Trump began his second term.The poll also found that 65% of Americans blame Trump’s policies more than factors outside his control for continued high prices.The findings come weeks before the midterm elections, with Republicans seeking to retain control of Congress and Trump campaigning at rallies across the country.Rising costs weigh on Trump’s economic recordAmericans have become increasingly concerned about paying for essentials such as food and petrol. Around half of US adults said they were “extremely” or “very” concerned about being able to fill their petrol tanks, up from 39% in July. A similar share expressed high concern about affording food.“I was hoping it would be better or different, but it’s not really good," Robert Gault, 66, a retired factory worker from Pennsylvania who describes himself as a Republican, told news agency AP.“Our president, I thought, was going to help the country, and so far he has not really seemed to have done that with the economy or in general. He’s not really done what I was hoping he would," Gault said. “He said, 'Make America Great Again.' And I have not seen him do that.”Pedro Sanchez, 52, a Trump voter who works in law enforcement in California, said rising fuel costs had reduced his disposable income.“Prices are ‘extremely exorbitant. Just the cost of everything is going up as a result of fuel,” Sanchez said, according to AP. “I used to have a lot more disposable income. I don’t have that any more. It’s gotten eaten up because of all these increases in the cost of everything.”About seven in 10 Americans said Trump’s handling of the cost of living had been “worse than expected”. Around six in 10 Republicans also disapproved of his performance on the issue, up from about half in April.Bethany Lnenicka, 41, a small-farm operator from Iowa and a political independent who typically votes Republican, said she had expected Trump’s second term to resemble his first.“I just do not feel like it has gotten a lot better,” she said.Kristen Slaven, 41, a Mississippi mental health therapist who typically votes Republican, also said the country had not moved in the right direction.“It definitely doesn’t feel like we have trended in the right direction,” Slaven said. “Obviously wars don’t help. When they’re necessary, I understand. But our focus on renaming bodies of water and pieces of land, that’s just stupid to me when people can't feed their family.”Tariffs, Iran war add to economic concernsTrump’s economic difficulties extend to his trade policy. Only about three in 10 Americans approve of his handling of trade negotiations with other countries, down from about four in 10 in March.Meanwhile, 64% said Trump had “gone too far” with new tariffs, compared with 58% in January.Americans also remain broadly unhappy with the war with Iran. About 69% said the war had not been worth fighting, up from 64% in July, while only 28% approved of Trump’s handling of Iran.Despite the wider frustration, Republicans remain more likely than the broader public to attribute high prices to factors outside Trump’s control. About 67% of Republicans said external factors were more responsible for high prices.Fred Naumann, 51, a Republican and longtime Trump supporter from Wisconsin, said inflation was difficult to address. He supports tariffs and the war with Iran, according to AP.Overall, only about three in 10 Americans approve of Trump’s performance as president, while roughly six in 10 say the country is “much” or “somewhat” worse off than when he began his second term.Border security remains one area where Trump retains relatively stronger support, with about half approving of his performance.Trump faces more economic blame than BidenTrump’s 26% economic approval rating is comparable with former President Joe Biden’s 28% rating in June 2022, when inflation had reached record levels during the Covid-19 pandemic.However, Americans were less likely to blame Biden’s policies for high prices before the 2022 midterm elections. In October that year, 44% said Biden’s policies were responsible for high prices, while 55% blamed factors outside his control.The comparison has also featured in views from Trump voters. Sanchez said Trump’s tariffs and the Iran war had directly affected the economy, while he viewed much of the economic disruption under Biden as stemming from the pandemic.“I think he has a lot to do with it. This war in Iran, the tariffs that he’s placing on other countries, obviously are affecting us,” Sanchez said. “Those two things are things he’s been directly involved in that directly affect the economy.”Separately, a Wall Street Journal poll cited by The Hill found Trump’s overall approval at 37%, the lowest for a president shortly before a midterm election in the Journal’s polling going back to George HW Bush.60% of respondents in that poll said Trump’s economic policies had worsened the economy, while 25% said they had improved it.The Journal poll, conducted from September 16 to 21 among 1,500 registered voters, had a margin of error of 2.5 percentage points.You use AI every day. articles.title: TN bypolls: Vijay’s TVK pays more money to voters than other parties do, Left parties allege
articles.summary: CHENNAI: CPM state secretary P Shanmugam on Thursday alleged that political parties were distributing cash to voters ahead of the Oct 6 bypolls in Tamil
articles.body: CHENNAI: CPM state secretary P Shanmugam on Thursday alleged that political parties were distributing cash to voters ahead of the Oct 6 bypolls in Tamil Nadu, claiming that villagers had told Left front campaigners that the ruling TVK was paying more money than other parties do. He demanded that the Election Commission look into the “confessional statement of the voters” and that political party leaders respond to the issue. However, TVK denied the allegation.Shanmugam said the widespread distribution of cash came to light when Left front leaders and cadres visited villages in Madurantakam assembly constituency to distribute pamphlets explaining why voters should support their candidates in the bypolls. "Villagers told us that all political parties were distributing cash for votes, with the ruling TVK paying the highest amount. They were also asking us for money," he said and described it “a confessional statement of the voters” on the prevailing cash-for-vote culture and how the TVK was leading in this front.TVK president and chief minister C Joseph Vijay had promised during the April assembly election campaign that his party would not distribute money to buy votes. He had reiterated the pledge during his bypoll campaigns, but the situation on the ground was different, Shanmugam said. Taking a dig at Vijay's description of TVK as a "thuyia sakthi" (pure force), Shanmugam said the party should explain the alleged cash distribution.Shanmugam was speaking to reporters on the sidelines of a statewide protest demanding the removal of chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar for allegedly acting "unilaterally and unlawfully" without consulting the other two election commissioners.CPI state secretary M Veerapandian echoed the same and said, “We found that members of other political parties are taking headcounts of voters in the two constituencies to distribute cash to them.”TVK national spokesman Pazha Selvakumar rejected Shanmugam's allegations, calling them "completely false". He said it was painful to hear such remarks from the Left parties, which had assured that their outside support to the TVK govt would continue. He said the parties should recall what had happened in bypolls from Thirumangalam to Erode East under previous regimes. Selvakumar said TVK had changed the political scenario by contesting elections democratically and opposed the practice of distributing money for votes.When reporters asked about the Left parties' allegations against its ally TVK, Tamil Nadu Congress Committee president Manickam Tagore said the ruling party had already made it clear that it was opposed to the practice of distributing cash for votes. articles.title: Boy arrested after teens' River Wear deaths released on bail
articles.summary: Jackson Duke, 17, and Luke Etheridge and Zara Shaw, both 16, died when a car entered the water.
articles.body:
A 17-year-old boy who was arrested after three teenagers died when a car entered the River Wear in Sunderland has been released on bail.

Sixteen-year-olds Luke Etheridge and Zara Shaw and 17-year-old Jackson Duke died after an Audi A3 came off the road at Panns Bank, near Wearmouth Bridge, and entered the river just before 13:30 BST on Tuesday.

The 17-year-old boy was arrested on suspicion of causing death by dangerous driving.

Northumbria Police has now confirmed he has been released on bail pending further inquiries.

The teenager had managed to reach safety and suffered non-serious injuries.

The investigation into the circumstances leading to the car entering the water continues.

Northumbria Police said on Wednesday no other vehicles were believed to have been involved.

Ch Supt Scott Cowie, area commander for Sunderland, said: "The last 24 hours have brought unimaginable agony and heartbreak for the loved ones of Luke, Jackson and Zara.

"All three had their whole futures ahead of them and will be hugely missed.

"We also recognise the impact that this tragedy has had upon the people of Sunderland and further afield, and know that you will continue to be there for one another."

On Wednesday, a spokesperson for Sunderland College said they were "deeply saddened" by the deaths of three of their students.

"This is a heartbreaking loss for our college community, and the wider city of Sunderland," a statement published on Facebook said.

articles.title: Former Traitors star calls it 'the hardest game I've ever played'
articles.summary: Joe Scott, from Southampton, reflects on his time in the castle during series three.
articles.body:
Former contestant on The Traitors Joe Scott has described the show as "the hardest game I've ever played".

The Southampton teacher said even hearing the opening music made him "nervous", as Celebrity Traitors returns for a second series.

Reflecting on his experience, the series three Faithful said: "I'd like to think I wouldn't jump to so many conclusions now, but it's really difficult".

Ahead of the first episode on Thursday he said: "I will definitely be watching. I am really looking forward to seeing how it all pans out."

Speaking to BBC Radio Solent, Scott said "one of the cutest" questions his students asked had been: "Sir, when you were on the show, who were the other celebrities in your series?

"I say I wasn't a celebrity but you definitely get a house point for that flattery."

Looking back on his time in the game, he said it had made everyone paranoid.

"Honestly you just over think every situation," he said.

"What you think is evidence is just people have slipped up and said something because they are nervous or they forgot something.

"You just latch onto it and think that means they are lying, that means they have tripped up."

He said it could be useful to have people that you trust "otherwise it's a very lonely game".

"You need to have those people where you think I am going to hedge my bets on them," he said.

"If they are a Traitor but you're friends with them and you're not going for them then they might not get rid of you anyway, so there is an advantage in believing in someone."

There are 21 celebrities taking part in total - two more than last year - and there will be an extra episode after the huge popularity of the previous series.

Scott said he expected James Blunt to do well, saying his dry sense of humour should make him strong at the Round Table.

"I always think that it's one of those where you might have your favourites and then you watch the game and you think actually I love this person just because of how they are playing the game," he added.

The extended 75-minute debut episode starts at 20:00 BST on Thursday, with the series continuing every Thursday and Friday throughout October.

articles.title: In 2020, Roger Daltrey and his family started Lakedown Brewing; three years later, the business opened its own brewery on his 600-acre Sussex farm, where he had created trout lakes decades earlier
articles.summary: A quiet corner of the East Sussex countryside, created decades ago by rock icon Roger Daltrey, has become a busy centre for craft beer production.
articles.body: A quiet corner of the East Sussex countryside, created decades ago by rock icon Roger Daltrey, has become a busy centre for craft beer production. Lakedown Brewing Co., founded in 2020 by The Who’s frontman with his family and entrepreneur Chris Rule, grew its business by opening a dedicated brewing facility on Daltrey’s 400-acre farm in Burwash. The musician bought the site in the 1970s as a peaceful place to escape from international concert tours. There, he dug four spring-fed trout lakes. Today, those same waters surround a modern family-run microbrewery and taproom. The business focuses on craft beers that are easy to drink and enjoy.From post-lockdown pint to family enterpriseThe idea for the brewery began during a quiet period after national pandemic restrictions. In an interview with Bite Sussex, co-founder Jamie Daltrey explained how a casual drink by the water helped start the family business. "We were enjoying a relaxing post lockdown pint together at the water's edge in the idyllic Lakedown Trout Fishery," Jamie Daltrey told Bite Sussex. "It was a perfect time and place for a beer!""We had a vision to create a local brewery that brought people together, celebrated the East Sussex countryside and made for easy, social drinking," he added. "Inspired by our surroundings and love of craft beer, we decided to make our own beers using the finest quality ingredients and create equally brilliant places to drink them in."The 41-year-old returned to East Sussex after working in the London television industry. He took over management of the Lakedown Trout Fishery in 2019, then co-founded the brewery the following year. The estate has a strong personal meaning for the family. Roger Daltrey first built the fishery in the 1970s as a place to get away from the demands of touring around the world with The Who. The family's creative background is also reflected in the brand. Its visual logo celebrates local wildlife while including subtle references to music.Focus on accessible local craft brewingLakedown Brewing Co. operates in a regional market with about 40 independent breweries. It has built its identity around sessionable, full-flavoured beers that are made for a wide range of drinkers. "Our beers are made for easy drinking, and are super fresh and sessionable," Jamie Daltrey told Bite Sussex. "All of Lakedown Brewing Co.'s beers are vegan and most are gluten-free. We use carefully sourced, quality ingredients that allow the beer the time it needs for a deliciously full-flavored brew." The brewery follows a grain-to-glass approach. It combines traditional brewing methods with modern production equipment. Its main range includes a Pilsner, English Pale, Pale Ale, NEIPA, Best Bitter, IPA, Porter, American Red and Vermont Pale Ale. The beers are available in cask, keg, bottle and can formats. The company sells directly through its website, including monthly subscription plans. It also serves local customers at its on-site Taproom in the Wealden Valley. Its beers are supplied to independent pubs, bars and bottle shops across Sussex. The family has also used the brand to support local cultural projects. According to company updates shared with Bite Sussex, Lakedown extended its sponsorship of the Fat Tuesday Music Festival to support the Hastings Fat Tuesday Club. The funding provides free creative music workshops and technical training for young people aged 12 to 18 at the Contemporary Music School in St Leonards. The new facility gives the family business room to increase production while keeping its main operations based on the East Sussex farm.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Arwal revenue official held for taking Rs16,000 bribe
articles.summary: Vigilance bureau arrests Arwal revenue official Shivmangal Prasad in Rs16,000 land measurement bribe trap; 105th trap case of 2026, probe on.
articles.body: Patna: The Vigilance Investigation Bureau (VIB) on Thursday arrested a revenue employee-cum-in-charge circle inspector of Arwal circle office for allegedly accepting a Rs16,000 bribe to conduct the measurement of a complainant’s ancestral land.The accused, Shivmangal Prasad, was caught during a trap operation at Ojha Bigha Mor in Arwal district in connection with a vigilance case registered on Sept 30.According to the bureau, complainant Rabindra Prasad of Umairabad village had applied online for the measurement of his ancestral land. He alleged that despite the application remaining pending for a long time, Shivmangal demanded money to process the measurement.The complaint was verified by the bureau, which found the bribery allegation prima facie true. Subsequently, a team led by DSP Mohd Wasim Firoz was constituted and laid a trap.Vigilance officials said Shivmangal was arrested while allegedly accepting the bribe amount. He will be produced before the Special Vigilance Court in Patna after interrogation.The bureau said the arrest was its 105th trap case of 2026, with 105 accused persons caught while allegedly accepting bribes. articles.summary: A celebration at Louisville's historic Chickasaw Park took an unexpected turn in November 2025 when officials revealed that an anonymous donor had given
articles.body: A celebration at Louisville's historic Chickasaw Park took an unexpected turn in November 2025 when officials revealed that an anonymous donor had given $5 million towards restoring the century-old public space.
